verses.text: What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision?
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?
God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged.
But if our unrighteousness commend the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous who taketh vengeance? (I speak as a man)
God forbid: for then how shall God judge the world?
For if the truth of God hath more abounded through my lie unto his glory; why yet am I also judged as a sinner?
And not rather, ( as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.
What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin;
As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one:
There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God.
They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one.
Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:
Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness:
Their feet are swift to shed blood:
Destruction and misery are in their ways:
And the way of peace have they not known:
There is no fear of God before their eyes.
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets;
Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference:
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith.
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also:
Seeing it is one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith.
Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law.

summary: Paul begins by answering the objection his own argument invites: if privilege does not exempt, then "What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision?" His answer is not dismissive but emphatic — "Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God" — and human failure cannot cancel divine fidelity: "shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar." He then refuses two twisted inferences: that God is "unrighteous who taketh vengeance" if human wrong somehow displays his right, and the slander that his gospel amounts to "Let us do evil, that good may come," of which he says only "whose damnation is just." The indictment then closes on everyone: "we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin," and he stitches together Israel's own Scriptures to prove it — "There is none righteous, no, not one," "There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God," "Their throat is an open sepulchre," "Their feet are swift to shed blood," "And the way of peace have they not known," "There is no fear of God before their eyes." The law's role in this scene is prosecutorial rather than remedial: it speaks "to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God," so that "by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin." At verse 21 the whole argument pivots on two words: "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets" — new in disclosure, not in intention. It comes "by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." The freedom is not cheapness, and Paul names the cost at once: God "hath set forth" Christ "to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God," so that God might be at once "just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus." Two consequences follow. Boasting is "excluded" — not by "law ... of works" but "by the law of faith" — and the door is one door for all, since God is not "the God of the Jews only" but "one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith." Paul ends by blocking the inference readers will rush to: "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law."
takeaways: The indictment is anatomical before it is abstract — throat, tongues, lips, mouth, feet, ways, eyes — so that sin is described as something the whole person does rather than a private interior fault. The law's first office here is diagnosis, not cure: "by the law is the knowledge of sin," and its aim is "that every mouth may be stopped."

Israel's privilege is affirmed, not revoked. "Unto them were committed the oracles of God" stands even after the verdict falls on all, and the argument that unbelief could void God's faithfulness is answered with "God forbid" — the reliability of God is never made to depend on the performance of those he called.

The gospel's newness is a newness of manifestation, not of plan: the righteousness "without the law" is nonetheless "witnessed by the law and the prophets." Paul claims the Scriptures as his witnesses rather than his opponents, which is why he can end with "we establish the law" rather than discard it.

"Justified freely by his grace" is not leniency waived through. The same sentence names a "propitiation through faith in his blood" and gives its purpose as declaring God's righteousness, so that he might be "just, and the justifier" — the chapter refuses to let mercy be purchased at the price of justice, or justice at the price of mercy.

"There is no difference" cuts both ways in this chapter: it levels the indictment ("all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God") and then levels the access ("one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith"). Because the ground is grace and not achievement, "boasting" is not discouraged but structurally "excluded."

crossRefs.label: Psalm 14:1-3 — there is none that doeth good, no, not one
crossRefs.why: The opening links of Paul's chain of testimony come from Israel's own book of prayer, where God looks down from heaven on the children of men and finds none who does good. Drawing the verdict from the psalter matters to the argument: the charge that "they are all under sin" is not an outsider's accusation but Israel's own worship turned into evidence.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 59:7-8 — their feet run to evil ... the way of peace they know not
crossRefs.why: Paul's lines "Their feet are swift to shed blood" and "the way of peace have they not known" are drawn from a prophetic passage where sin is described as a barrier that has hidden God's face, and which then answers itself with the promise of a Redeemer coming to Zion. The borrowed language carries its original shape: indictment that is a prelude to rescue, not a closing of the case.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 2:16 — a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the same claim in a hotter context, where the pressure is table fellowship and circumcision rather than a general anthropology, and he presses it to its edge: "if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain." Read alongside Romans 3, it shows that the phrase "the deeds of the law" is being deployed against a specific claim on God, and it is the passage most often set against Romans 3:31.

crossRefs.label: Romans 4:3 — Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness
crossRefs.why: Chapter 3 asserts that "boasting" is "excluded" and immediately faces the obvious test case: the father of the nation. Paul argues that Abraham was reckoned righteous before circumcision and apart from wages owed, which is the working out of "justified freely by his grace" and the reason he can insist he does not "make void the law."

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 9:12 — by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place
crossRefs.why: The word "propitiation" in "a propitiation through faith in his blood" carries the imagery of the covering of the ark where atoning blood was sprinkled, and this passage makes that sanctuary logic explicit while also speaking of redemption for transgressions committed under the earlier covenant. It supplies the ritual grammar behind Paul's compressed phrase about "sins that are past, through the forbearance of God."

crossRefs.label: James 2:24 — by works a man is justified, and not by faith only
crossRefs.why: James uses the same vocabulary of justification, the same example of Abraham, and reaches a verbally opposite conclusion, insisting that "faith without works is dead." The two texts are the hinge of the historic dispute, and any reading of "justified by faith without the deeds of the law" has to say what kind of works each writer has in view and whether they are describing the same moment.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic reading takes "the deeds of the law" in "a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law" to mean works done apart from grace — above all the observances urged as a claim upon God, which is why circumcision frames the chapter at both ends — rather than the whole life of obedience that grace itself produces. On this reading faith is the root and beginning of justification, entirely unearned ("Being justified freely by his grace"), but the faith that justifies is a living faith working through love; the text says "by faith," never "by faith alone," and Paul's own closing refusal, "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law," is taken as blocking any conclusion that leaves obedience outside the shape of salvation.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read "without the deeds of the law" broadly, as excluding every human work from the ground of justification rather than only ceremonial or ungraced ones. Since "all have sinned," faith is the empty hand that receives Christ, and works follow as the fruit of justification rather than as any part of its basis; on this reading, if grace-enabled works contributed to the verdict itself, "Where is boasting then? It is excluded" would be undone. "We establish the law" is then understood to mean the law is upheld and honoured because Christ has satisfied it, and because faith produces the obedience the law always sought. Both traditions agree that justification begins wholly in grace, that no one places God in his debt, and that a justified life is meant to bear real obedience.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "the righteousness of God ... manifested" and "justified freely by his grace" as describing a genuine interior renewal rather than a change of legal standing only: God does not merely reckon the sinner righteous while leaving him what he was, but makes him righteous by a righteousness truly given and possessed, though never owned as an achievement. Justification on this reading has a beginning and a growth, can be lost by grave sin and restored, and is inseparable from the charity poured into the heart — so that "the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" names a God who heals what he pardons.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpretation emphasises that the vocabulary here is courtroom vocabulary — "that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God" is a verdict scene — and reads justification as a declarative act in which God credits the righteousness of Christ to the believer while the believer is still a sinner, precisely so that God can be "just, and the justifier." Renewal is affirmed as certain and necessary but distinguished as sanctification, kept separate from justification so that assurance rests on Christ's finished work rather than on measurable interior progress. Both traditions hold that grace is the sole source, that faith is not a human achievement, and that the justified are genuinely destined for holiness.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the catena of verses 10 to 18 — "There is none righteous, no, not one" and "There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God" — the Catholic reading takes the indictment as universal in scope and devastating in effect while holding that sin wounds human nature without destroying it. The image of God in man remains, reason and will are weakened rather than annihilated, and the description of a race that does not seek God is a description of humanity left to itself, not a denial that grace going before a person can genuinely heal and free the will to respond.

counterpoint.summary: In the Reformed stream especially, these verses are read as the clearest scriptural statement of a corruption reaching every faculty — mind ("none that understandeth"), will ("none that seeketh after God"), speech, conduct and reverence — such that no one turns to God unless God first grants new life, and any residual capacity to initiate the turning would blunt the force of "they are all under sin." Other Protestants hold a prevenient-grace account much closer to the Catholic reading, in which grace restores a real capacity to respond that sin had made impossible. Both traditions affirm that no one is justified apart from grace and that the initiative belongs entirely to God.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
